questions.q: What did Darwin's travels suggest about facial expressions?
a: Basic emotions look the same across different cultures
Each culture teaches its own set of expressions
Only trained observers can read emotions accurately
Facial cues are useless for spotting deception
questions.why: The first lesson says Darwin found people from various cultures could correctly read the feelings in the photographs he showed.

questions.q: According to the summary, how often is the average adult lied to?
a: Between 10 and 200 times a day
About once or twice a week
Roughly five times a month
Almost never by people they know
questions.why: The second lesson cites studies putting daily deception at 10 to 200 instances, many of them harmless white lies.

questions.q: Why is lying more common in the modern world?
a: Technology lets us communicate without meeting anyone's eyes
People are naturally less honest than in past centuries
Laws against deception are rarely enforced today
Schools no longer teach children to tell the truth
questions.why: The summary says phone and video communication removes eye contact and physical contact, opening more room for dishonesty.

questions.q: What does Meyer recommend instead of cornering someone you suspect of lying?
a: Connecting with them so they feel safe telling the truth
Pressing them until they finally confess
Threatening to expose the lie in public
Ending the relationship without discussion
questions.why: She writes that cornering an opponent makes lying likely, while a real connection makes truth far more likely.

questions.q: Why do people tell white lies, according to the summary?
a: To keep relationships smooth and fit social norms
To extract money from strangers
To test whether others are paying attention
To avoid all forms of responsibility
questions.why: The second lesson says white lies are told in good faith and help us maintain relationships and fit into society.
